findings.issue_text: Google Calendar CalendarService writes `parseRefreshTokenResponse` output (a safeParse result wrapper `{success, data}`) directly into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, corrupting the stored credential so access_token/refresh_token/expiry_date reads fail after first token refresh

`minimumTokenResponseSchema` is a plain `z.object` in strip mode, so with credential sharing enabled the parsed output contains only `access_token`, wiping refresh_token, expiry_date, instance_url, and scope from persisted credentials (Google, Office365, Salesforce, Zoom)

In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key `"[object Object]"`, so the second overwrites the first, no expiry field is validated, and a junk key is added; needs `.catchall()` or `z.record()`

parseRefreshTokenResponse sets `refresh_token` to the literal string `"refresh_token"` when absent, which gets persisted and makes all future refreshes send `refresh_token=refresh_token`, permanently breaking the integration (also affects the non-sync path)

refreshOAuthTokens sync branch returns a raw fetch `Response` while callers expect app-specific shapes (Google `res?.data.access_token`, HubSpot `HubspotToken.expiresIn`, Zoho axios-style `tokenInfo.data.error`), causing TypeErrors or undefined values when CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set; the untyped `refreshFunction: () => any` hides this from the compiler

zoho-bigin CalendarService passes `credentialId` as the third argument where all other call sites pass `credential.userId`, so the sync endpoint receives a credential ID in the `calcomUserId` field and looks up the wrong user

Salesforce CalendarService performs an unconditional token refresh POST plus a `prisma.credential.update` on every service instantiation with no expiry check, adding a round-trip and DB write per booking operation and risking Salesforce OAuth rate limits

Salesforce CalendarService persists the freshly obtained token but still constructs `new jsforce.Connection({...})` from the unchanged `credentialKey`, so the connection uses the old access token and instance URL

Salesforce CalendarService uses `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` as a success check, which is unreliable (empty over HTTP/2 and in many runtimes), throwing on successful responses and passing some failures; should use `!response.ok`
app-credential webhook compares the webhook secret with `!==`, a non-constant-time comparison on a shared secret; should use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers

The outbound POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT in refreshOAuthTokens carries no authentication or signature (only calcomUserId and appSlug), so anyone who can reach the endpoint can request any user's access token

refreshOAuthTokens returns the sync response without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint is passed downstream as if it were a token payload (e.g. an HTML error body parsed as tokens)

app-credential webhook calls `schema.parse(req.body)` unguarded, so a malformed body throws ZodError out of the handler and returns a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400; use `safeParse` or try/catch

app-credential webhook calls `symmetricDecrypt(...)` and `JSON.parse(...)` unguarded, so a wrong encryption key, truncated ciphertext, or non-JSON plaintext yields an opaque 500 instead of a 400 'invalid keys payload'

app-credential webhook uses `findFirst` followed by `create`, a check-then-act race where two concurrent syncs for the same (userId, appSlug) both create duplicate credential rows; there is no unique constraint on (userId, appId) — use a transaction or unique index with `upsert`
app-credential webhook handler accepts any HTTP method, so a GET with the right header will mutate credentials; it should reject anything but POST

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` in packages/lib/constants.ts is `string | undefined` (the raw value of CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY) rather than a boolean, risking the secret being serialized/inlined into client-side bundles; coerce with `!!(...)`

zoomvideo VideoApiAdapter hardcodes the app slug as `"zoomvideo"` (the directory name) instead of the registered slug `"zoom"`, so the sync endpoint receives an identifier that doesn't match `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`; slugs are hardcoded literals rather than read from each app's config.json

No tests accompany the feature — unit tests over `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (sync on/off, missing refresh_token, unknown-key stripping), `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, and the app-credential webhook are missing
Salesforce CalendarService's `if (!accessTokenParsed.success) return Promise.reject(...)` is dead code because `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on parse failure, so `success` is always true

office365calendar CalendarService removed the `console.error` that logged the zod error and raw Microsoft response on parse failure, losing diagnostic detail behind a generic 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' throw

zoho-bigin api/add.ts replaced `${appConfig.slug}` with a hardcoded `zoho-bigin` in the redirect URI, which can drift from config.json and the callback path, and likely leaves the `appConfig` import unused

The .env.example comment says the encryption key 'must be 32 bytes for AES256' but suggests `openssl rand -base64 24` (a 32-character string); it should state 32 characters, or self-hosters will use `rand -base64 32` and get a 44-char key that fails `createDecipheriv`

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential webhook compares the webhook secret with `!==`, a non-constant-time comparison on a shared secret; should use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers

adjudication.rationale:
In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated via a direct inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) { ... }
```

This is a normal JS/TS string comparison (`!==`), which is not guaranteed to be constant-time. For a shared-secret webhook authentication mechanism, this can theoretically enable timing attacks against the secret value. The diff indeed introduces this pattern and does not use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (or equivalent) to mitigate timing-based secret disclosure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The outbound POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT in refreshOAuthTokens carries no authentication or signature (only calcomUserId and appSlug), so anyone who can reach the endpoint can request any user's access token

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, the code does a `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug }) })` and does not include any authentication material (no shared secret header, no signature/HMAC, no bearer token, etc.). The only parameters sent are `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, so any party that can reach that endpoint could submit the same parameters; if the endpoint returns tokens based on those values (as implied by the comment “The response should only contain the access token and expiry date”), there is no request-level protection from this caller side. This lack of authentication is directly verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens returns the sync response without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint is passed downstream as if it were a token payload (e.g. an HTML error body parsed as tokens)

adjudication.rationale: Real issue. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when credential sync is enabled it does `const response = await fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` and immediately `return response;` with no `response.ok`/status handling. Multiple callers treat the return value as a successful token result (or at least proceed to parse it) rather than as a potentially failed HTTP response. For example, Google Calendar’s `refreshAccessToken` assigns `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` and then uses `const token = res?.data;` (which won’t exist on a `fetch` Response, and would also silently ignore non-2xx). Office365 passes the returned Response into `handleErrorsJson`, but that still means error responses from the sync endpoint are not handled centrally in `refreshOAuthTokens`. So a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint can propagate to downstream parsing/usage as if it were a valid token refresh result, causing runtime failures or attempts to parse error bodies as token payloads.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` handler, the code does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then branches to `update` vs `create`. That check-then-act sequence is not atomic, so two concurrent webhook requests for the same `(userId, appSlug/appId)` can both observe “no credential” and both call `prisma.credential.create(...)`. Whether that results in duplicate rows or a unique-constraint error depends on schema constraints (not shown in this diff), but the race condition itself is verifiably present in the diff and should be addressed via an atomic upsert/transaction and/or a unique index with proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app-credential webhook handler accepts any HTTP method, so a GET with the right header will mutate credentials; it should reject anything but POST

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the exported `handler` never checks `req.method`. After the shared-secret header check, it immediately parses `req.body` via Zod and proceeds to decrypt and then `prisma.credential.update/create`, regardless of HTTP verb. Therefore any method that can carry a body (including a GET sent with a JSON body by some clients/proxies) and the correct header/secret can trigger credential mutation. There is no explicit rejection of non-POST methods (e.g., `405`).
